AbstractText.Label: BACKGROUND
AbstractText.content: Inhaled corticosteroids and long-acting beta-agonists (LABAs) are recommended for treating moderate to severe persistent asthma. The Food and Drug Administration has issued a black box warning (BBW) for LABAs.

AbstractText.Label: OBJECTIVE
AbstractText.content: To investigate physician knowledge of the BBW and its effect on the practice of specialists (pulmonologists and allergists) and primary care physicians (PCPs) (internists and family physicians).

AbstractText.Label: METHODS
AbstractText.content: A total of 1,107 physicians responded to a questionnaire to determine their awareness of the BBW and whether it changed their practice.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: The group comprised 429 pulmonologists (38.8%), 395 allergists (35.7%), 141 internists (12.7%), 132 family physicians (11.9%), and 10 pediatricians (0.9%). Comparing specialists with PCPs, there was approximately a 10% difference in the rate of knowledge concerning the BBW (99.0% vs 90.8%, P < .001). Approximately a quarter of specialists agreed with the BBW compared with 52.9% of family physicians and 40.3% of internists. Twice as many PCPs vs specialists agreed with the warning (45.6% vs 24.2%, P < .001). The PCPs were more likely to alter their prescribing habits than were specialists (40.1% vs 34.6%, P < .005). Specialists were more likely to discuss the warning with patients than were PCPs (87.4% vs 64.8%, P < .001). For mild persistent asthma, most respondents chose inhaled corticosteroids as the preferred first-line therapy, but 11.4% of PCPs and 2.1% of specialists identified LABA monotherapy as their first choice. For moderate to severe asthma, the pattern of response was similar.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSION
AbstractText.content: Although most physicians were aware of the BBW for LABAs, there was a difference in how specialists and PCPs approached it and altered their prescribing habits.
